newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Canada seen pursuing diplomacy, trade in Manila.
newsitem.headline: Canada seen pursuing diplomacy, trade in Manila.

text.p: Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chretien and an army of businessmen will descend on Manila on Tuesday seeking business opportunities.
Chretien will lead a 350-member delegation hoping to capitalise on growing interest in investment throughout the Pacific Rim.

Officially, he will also assume leadership of the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum from the Philippines. Unofficially, most of the business will involve negotiating or cementing millions of dollars in trade deals.
Officials said Chretien's combination of the two roles highlights the private sector's dominance of APEC.

"We are very pleased about this aspect. The Philippines is really focussed on the business element, trying to get them (businessmen) engaged in APEC," Judith St. George, Canada's senior trade commissioner in the Philippines, told Reuters.
St. George and other Canadian diplomats in Manila said Chretien's Philippine visit was expected to culminate in a series of business deals that would promote bilateral trade.
Chretien begins Canada's one-year term as APEC leader after a handover ceremony in Manila on Tuesday.

APEC comprises 18 economies from Asia, Australia and the Americas that hope to achieve free regional trade by 2020. As leader, Canada will host the annual APEC summit and coordinate the group's various activities during the year.
Philippine officials said Chretien's trade mission meant the private sector would continue to play an important role within the group.

"It is a good signal that they are bringing Canadian businessmen...very much in line with our philosophy of economic diplomacy and our belief that APEC means business," a Philippine foreign affairs official said.

The Philippines, as 1996 chairman, actively promoted the private sector to the forefront of the APEC process. It pushed for the appointment of 50 top businessmen from the Asia-Pacific region as advisers to the grouping.

Manila's philosophy on APEC was to let businessmen get together and strike deals, and free trade would automatically follow. It put this into practice by organising a businessmen's summit along with the annual APEC summit in November, where deal-making and networking topped the agenda.

Canada has said it will hold the 1997 APEC summit in Vancouver in the last two weeks of November. Analysts said it would be a crucial year for the trade grouping as it begins implementing its ambitious plans.

The Manila summit adopted a plan on how to meet the goal of free trade by 2010 for rich countries, and by 2020 for developing nations in the region. Member nations are expected to submit their responses in Canada.
Chretien arrives in Manila from Seoul with "Team Canada", the term given his trade missions. He will later visit Bangkok.

Canadian diplomats said that, unlike other Western countries that sought to crown their trade missions with deals worth billions of dollars, Chretien's Manila visit was expected to produce smaller deals.

"They would be fairly small, many below one million dollars, but that's the nature of this market. And we are proud that small companies can do well in this market because traditionally in Asia it is not easy for small firms," St. George said.

Estimates of how much more Canada hopes to export to the Philippines after the visit were not available, but officials said the exports would be mainly in telecommunications equipment and in niche areas like software development.
The Philippines hopes to sell more textiles and industrial machinery to Canada.
In 1995, bilateral trade was at C$825 million with the Philippines at a surplus, showing exports of C$497 million (US $369 million). Last year's figures were not yet available.
